name: Flaxseed
summary: Flaxseed is the seed of the flax plant, eaten whole, ground or pressed into oil. This page lists what people say flaxseed does and what a Roman medical writer believed; each claim can be checked against the research when you choose.
inIt: Flaxseed is one of the richest sources of alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, a plant omega-3 fat) and of lignans, with a good amount of fibre and protein.
Its main lignan is secoisolariciresinol diglucoside. Flax lignans are called phytoestrogens, plant compounds that resemble the hormone oestrogen in structure.
The UK food table (CoFID) has no entry for flaxseed or linseed, so this page gives no per-100 g figures from it. Lignans and other plant compounds are not measured in food tables.
processing: In a 2009 meta-analysis of 28 trials, whole flaxseed and lignan supplements lowered total and LDL cholesterol a little, but flaxseed oil did not. Oil has the omega-3 fat but not the lignans or fibre.

lore.belief: Celsus wrote that a throat ulcer which vinegar could not heal could be treated with linseed pounded and mixed with sweet wine.

sources.title: Celsus, De Medicina 4.9.1 (ulcers of the throat), Loeb translation (Spencer)
sources.author: Celsus

lore.belief: For an enlarged spleen, Celsus described a plaster of linseed and nasturtium seeds with wine and oil added, applied on the outside.

sources.title: Celsus, De Medicina 4.16.3 (disease of the spleen), Loeb translation (Spencer)
sources.author: Celsus

lore.belief: For long-lasting dysentery, Celsus advised a decoction of linseed injected into the bowel, to ease the pain and soften the ulcers there.
Celsus listed linseed among the meals used for hot poultices, and said the power to soften and disperse inflammation belongs especially to plasters of linseed or fenugreek.

sources.title: Celsus, De Medicina 2.33.5-6 (poultices and plasters), Loeb translation (Spencer)
sources.author: Celsus

lore.belief: Celsus counted linseed among the substances that most strongly disperse matter collected in the body, and among those that draw out diseased matter.

sources.title: Celsus, De Medicina 5.11.1 and 5.12.1 (dispersing and drawing remedies), Loeb translation (Spencer)
sources.author: Celsus

unknowns: Whether eating whole or ground flaxseed changes health outcomes beyond small shifts in blood pressure and cholesterol: this page does not review the trials.
Whether the plant lignans in flaxseed act like a hormone in the body: the reviews describe them as phytoestrogens, but this page does not settle what that means for any one person.

How safe large amounts of flaxseed are for people with hormone-related conditions, or who are pregnant: this page found no source to cite, so it says nothing either way. If this applies to you, talk to your doctor.
